The '''square root of 3''' is the positive [[real number]] that, when multiplied by itself, gives the number [[3 (number)|3]]. It is denoted mathematically as '''<math display="inline">\sqrt {3}</math>''' or '''<math>3^{1/2}</math>'''. It is more precisely called the '''principal square root of 3''' to distinguish it from the negative number with the same property. The [[square root]] of 3 is an [[irrational number]]. It is also known as '''Theodorus's constant''', after [[Theodorus of Cyrene]], who proved its irrationality.<ref>{{Cite web |title=square root of 3 |url=https://planetmath.org/squarerootof3 |access-date=2025-07-23 |website=planetmath.org}}</ref>

In 2013, its numerical value in decimal notation was computed to ten billion digits.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Komsta |first=Łukasz |date=December 2013 |title=Computations &#124; Łukasz Komsta |url=http://www.komsta.net/computations |access-date=September 24, 2016 |website=komsta.net |publisher=WordPress|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002181125/http://www.komsta.net/computations|archive-date=2023-10-02|url-status=dead}}</ref> Its [[decimal expansion]], written here to 60 decimal places, is given by {{OEIS2C|id=A002194}}:
:{{gaps|1.73205|08075|68877|29352|74463|41505|87236|69428|05253|81038|06280|55806}}

[[Archimedes]] reported a range for its value: <math display="inline">(\frac{1351}{780})^{2}>3>(\frac{265}{153})^{2}
</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Knorr |first=Wilbur R. |author-link=Wilbur Knorr |date=June 1976 |title=Archimedes and the measurement of the circle: a new interpretation |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00348496 |journal=[[Archive for History of Exact Sciences]] |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=115–140 |doi=10.1007/bf00348496 |jstor=41133444 |mr=0497462 |url-access=subscription |access-date=November 15, 2022 |via=SpringerLink |s2cid=120954547}}</ref> 

The upper limit '''<math display="inline">\frac {1351}{780}</math>''' is an accurate approximation for '''<math>\sqrt {3}</math>''' to <math display="inline">\frac {1}{608,400}</math> (six decimal places, relative error <math display="inline">3 \times 10^{-7}</math>) and the lower limit '''<math display="inline">\frac {265}{153}</math>''' to <math display="inline">\frac {2}{23,409}</math> (four decimal places, relative error <math display="inline">1\times 10^{-5}</math>).

==Rational approximations==
{{See also|Square root algorithms}}
The square root of 3 is an [[irrational number]], meaning it can not be exactly represented as a fraction {{tmath|x/y}} where {{tmath|x}} and {{tmath|y}} are [[integer]]s. However, it can be approximated arbitrarily closely by such [[rational number]]s.

Particularly good approximations are the integer solutions of [[Pell's equation]]s,
:<math>x^2 - 3y^2 = 1</math>
which can be algebraically rearranged into the form
:<math>\frac{x}{y} = \sqrt{3 + \frac{1}{y^2}} .</math>

The first several solutions are given below:

These approximations also appear among the convergents of its [[continued fraction]].

==Geometry and trigonometry==

{{multiple image
| align             = left
| total_width       = 420
| image1            = Equilateral triangle with height square root of 3.svg
| image2            = Root 3 Hexagon.svg
| footer            = 
| direction         = 
| alt1              = 
| caption1          = The [[Altitude (triangle)|height]] of an [[equilateral triangle]] with edge length 2 is {{sqrt|3}}. Also, the long [[Cathetus|leg]] of a [[Special right triangle#30°–60°–90° triangle|30-60-90 triangle]] with [[hypotenuse]] 2.
| caption2          = And, the height of a regular [[hexagon]] with sides of length 1
}}
[[File:Square root of 3 in cube.svg|thumb|The [[space diagonal]] of the [[unit cube]] is {{sqrt|3}}.]]

The square root of 3 can be found as the [[Cathetus|leg]] length of an equilateral triangle that encompasses a circle with a diameter of 1.

If an [[equilateral triangle]] with sides of length 1 is cut into two equal halves, by bisecting an internal angle across to make a right angle with one side, the right angle triangle's [[hypotenuse]] is length one, and the sides are of length '''<math display="inline">\frac{1}{2}</math>''' and '''<math display="inline">\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}</math>'''. From this, <math display="inline">\tan{60^\circ}=\sqrt{3}</math>, <math display="inline">\sin{60^\circ}=\frac {\sqrt{3}}{2}</math>, and <math display="inline">\cos{30^\circ}=\frac {\sqrt{3}}{2}</math>.

The square root of 3 also appears in algebraic expressions for various other [[Exact trigonometric constants|trigonometric constants]], including<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wiseman |first=Julian D. A. |date=June 2008 |title=Sin and Cos in Surds |url=http://www.jdawiseman.com/papers/easymath/surds_sin_cos.html |access-date=November 15, 2022 |website=JDAWiseman.com}}</ref> the sines of other angles. For example, <math display="inline">\tan{15^\circ}=2-\sqrt{3}</math> and <math display="inline">\tan{75^\circ}=2+\sqrt{3}</math>.

It is the distance between parallel sides of a regular [[hexagon]] with sides of length 1. It is also the length of the longest side of a triangle formed from two adjacent sides of a regular hexagon; following from the law of cosines:

<math display=block>\begin{align}
c^2 &= a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos\gamma, \\[3mu]
\end{align}</math>

Since each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°, we can substitute 120° for <math>\gamma</math> in the equation above.

<math display=block>\begin{align}
c^2 &= 1^2 + 1^2 - 2ab\cos 120^\circ \\
    &= 1 + 1 - 2(-1/2) \\
    &= 2 - (-1) \\
    &= 3 \\

c = \sqrt 3
\end{align}</math>

It is the length of the [[space diagonal]] of a unit [[cube]].
[[File:Vesica piscis2.svg|thumb|The areas in blue{{snd}} an equilateral triangle and a segment{{snd}} form together a sector of one sixth of the circle (60°)]]
The [[vesica piscis]] has a major axis to minor axis ratio equal to <math>\sqrt{3}:1</math>. This can be shown by constructing two equilateral triangles within it.

==Applications==

===Electrical engineering===

The square root of 3 plays a pivotal role in studies of [[three-phase electric power]]. <ref>{{cite web|url=https://relaytraining.com/the-complete-guide-to-the-square-root-of-three-in-power-calculations/?srsltid=AfmBOor35eBbPO9thQ7fahsa8j9wi-Qbq0GNWoEiGQPj4Jy2u9vZyA6i|title=The Complete Guide to the Square Root of Three in Power Calculations|publisher=Relay Training}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://schnackel.com/insight/whitepapers/general-white-papers/why-the-square-root-of-three|title=Why the √3?|publisher=Schnackel}}</ref>
